subject: general
question: In a metallic wire obeying Ohm's Law, if the resistance remains constant, reducing the potential difference across its terminals to one-half of its former value will result in what change in the current flowing through it?

options.text: The current reduces to one-half of its former value.
The current reduces to one-fourth of its former value.

solution:
The correct answer is __**The current reduces to one-half of its former value**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Ohm's Law** states that the electric **current (I)** flowing through a metallic conductor is **directly proportional** to the **potential difference (V)** applied across its terminals, provided that physical conditions like **temperature** and **pressure** remain constant.
 
• The relationship is mathematically expressed as **V = IR**, where **R** is the **resistance** of the conductor. 
 
• When the **resistance (R)** remains **constant**, the current can be calculated using the formula **I = V / R**. This implies that the current is linearly dependent on the voltage.
 
• If the **potential difference** is reduced to **one-half (1/2)** of its original value, the new current (I') becomes **(V/2) / R**, which is equivalent to **1/2 * (V/R)**. *Hence, the statement that the current reduces to one-half of its former value is correct.*
